The criticism about issues is mostly true but despite all that this is still easily the best game ever!

Of all 'open world' games this one comes closest to actually being that, a 'world' in medieval Bohemia that is open to your decisions and preferences. 
Of course you are forced into some main storyline and without doing it it's not worth playing the game, I mean you could for a while but to really get your character Henry going you just have to go through what the developers intended for him to experience.

And that's the other thing, there's no character creation, you are Henry, son of a blacksmith, uprooted from his village life by a marauding army. 
Most things in the game present multiple angles to tackle them, so in a way you can shape his character by way of your decisions but it's always Henry, you're playing his story and his reactions in dialogues and cutscenes may not reflect the route you choose to take.

This is a truly fantastic game that had me hooked for months. To be able to say that about a game where you are simply playing as a blacksmiths son in medieval Bohemia is kind of surprising but it's true.

As mentioned you play a blacksmiths son called Henry who lives in the small town of Skalitz, who's simple existence gets turned upside down when an army from Hungary shows up one day and burns and plunders his village, killing his parents in front of him. Henry escapes and gets caught up in the ensuing events and has to quickly adapt to his harsh new reality.

Kingdom Come is an open world RPG but it feels really unique due to the fact that it's grounded in historical reality rather than the usual fantasy or sci-fi based worlds and stories that are generally typical of the genre. Henry is just an average guy. He's not going  on a quest to end up a king or to save the world. He isn't going to cut his way through hordes of enemies or be a special "Chosen One". He can't even read when you begin the game. This is why Kingdom Come feels so unique. You're just an average guy who has to learn and do things the hard way.

You can level up all sorts of skills from combat skills like sword fighting, or physical stats like strength and agility and there are even a range of skills like horseriding, lockpicking and even drinking. Levelling up earns you perks some of which are very useful others come with a price such as being able to run faster but at the cost of losing stamina quicker. When you start the game Henry can barely swing a sword or shoot a bow so everything can be difficult. Put in the effort though and you can mold Henry into a capable warrior.

The combat is difficult to grasp at first but rewarding when you get better. Unlike in Skyrim, for example, you're not going to be able tear apart big groups of enemies even when you have levelled up your combat abilites. Even towards the end of the game I still got caught out once or twice by a band of simple armed peasants, simply because they could use their numbers against me. Combat requires a bit of skill as you try and create an opening to strike an opponent. Even one and one fights can be a long slog if your opponent is a skilled fighter. Taking on more opponents is even harder. I did find the terrible lock on system didn't help though. It's fine when fighting one or two guys but with groups the camera swings about a lot trying to focus on the different enemies which can be disorientating.

I feel this games strongest point is it's great quests. The main quests are quite interesting with multiple outcomes or ways to complete the quest. Even the side quests are quite well developed and well worth doing. If your not careful though you can fail some quests with some even having an unseen time limit. The world in Kingdom Come won't always wait for you so if someone tells you you need to go somewhere by a certain time you better take heed. 

The games story is really good too with some great characters. Henry himself is a likeable guy and you meet a lot of well developed characters like the medieval party boy Hans Capon or the unconventional priest Godwin. The games story comes with lots of political intrigue and interesting scenarios.

There are some things that let the game down. Most prominently is that it can be quite buggy. I've got stuck in scenery or fell through the floor a few times. The game has gotten stuck on loading screens a few times which I had to close down the game to escape. Some of the dialogue scenes towards the end of the game were quite buggy with missing commands instead of dialogue or characters being invisible during a conversation. Compared to some of the stuff I've heard my experience wasn't too bad. To be fair a lot of bugs have been fixed but there still a lot there. 

Another thing I didn't like was the save system. In this game you save when starting or completing a Main or Side quest, when you sleep or by using a consumable. Not granted your never far from a bed and the save consumble can be purchased easy enough or even brewed cheaply but I did have a quite a few times where I got caught out and died unexpectedly which caused me to lose a load of progress. When that happens it can be really frustrating.

Overall though I still really loved this game and I'm glad things have been left open fora sequel. As much as I liked this game though I think it's fair to say it may not be for everyone. It can be quite a slow game and can be frustratingly difficult at the start particularly. The intro is also really long so you've got about 2-3 hours before the game lets you loose. But that said if anything about this game sounds appealing to you then give it a try as it's honestly become one of my favourite RPGs that I have ever played.

This game is definitely not for everyone, But if you love historical accuracy, HEMA (Historical European Martial Arts) you will fall in love with this game to the bones.. This game is different from any other RPG i've played before, its not about going out and do some quest all the time, its not about become the Dragonborn or the choosen one, you are no one in this game, you're just a poor blacksmith's son.. its about living the life of Henry. What will you do if you are a dude living at year 1403 ? 

         So what is this game about? Its a story about Henry a blackshmith son who sucks at everything, literally everything.. You can't read, you can't ride a horse properly, you can't hande a bow properly, you can't even cut a 2 cm wood stick with a sword.. Well what should you do then? Practice practice and practice.. Every morning i woke up at 7 a.m then i wash my face and equip my gears, then i go to the tavern to get some breakfast, then at 9 a.m i went to Captain Bernard to sparring sword with him so i can become a better swordman, then i check my journal book to see what mission or side mission should i do, if im too lazy to do some mission usually i went to the woods and hunt some rabbits, boars, deers or bandits.. [h1] What is an RPG "open world" game?? I had no clue... [/h1] 

I feel like you need to understand the place where I'm at in order to better understand me and the experience with this game so bear with me for a little bit. My last gaming experience was my PS2 prob in 2002-2003 in college, I remember playing Duke Nukem and the first Metal Gear solid. Then life happened. I was just too busy to give games time in my life. Then COVID happened. Due to having access to free games (bought the NVIDIA Shield and it came with some), I decided to start playing some. My very first experience was with Spec Ops The Line, and OMG did that leave an impression on me. When the credits rolled, I remember just sitting there, not moving, remote still in hand and my mind really REALLY F'd. What did I just play? What have games ascended to nowadays?... I have to tell you that if you call yourself a gamer and you haven't played Spec Ops The Line, then I don't even know what you're doing with your life. That game is not about the graphics or gameplay, it's about the last 5 minutes of the story and how that truly makes a twist in the protagonist story and makes you question EVERYTHING that happened on that game. Needless to say, do me a favor and go play that game. So I was hooked. I needed to explore this NEW world of gaming that I had stumbled across. 

Enter Kingdom Come: Deliverance..

My father and I always enjoyed anything medieval (movies mostly) so anything with knight armors and a good open field of battle where limbs are being hacked, has my attention. I came across the KCD page on steam and well, had to have it. I started playing it and within the first 5-10 minutes I was filled with regret. I couldn't manage the controls, or rather I didn't know how to work them, I tried to fight some dude and got my ass kicked, I was given chores and had no idea what to do. Think about a toddler trying to tie their shoes without knowing how and no help. I thought it was not what I wanted. I wanted action, I wanted to fight, I wanted something easy. What is this thing I had gotten myself into? I couldn't get my money back cause it was way past the time to return it. Oh well, I guess I have no other choice but to give it some time and let the story develop and see if I'm going to stick around for more....was my thought.

Sooo glad I did.....

I tried to read a bit about it to see if it was indeed worth it to stick around. Then I read it was an RPG....What the heck is that?...google "what is an RPG?"....hmm interesting. Let's keep pushing through and give it more time, I already paid for it, I might as well get some of my money in playtime.

The tides turned....

I reached a point in the game where I was given a "tournament quest"... just enroll in the tourney and win it!!, easy right? nope. Kept getting my ass handed to me over and over. This took me to the Reddit page of the game where I asked for help about how to fight in this game. This is when EVERYTHING changed for me about this game. The short answer from the people there was to level up my character. Holy heck what a difference did that make. I went from peasant to superhero and was able to fight anyone anywhere. Don't expect to be good at anything in this game from the get go. You WILL suck at everything you try to do until you get Henry some experience in it.

This game is based on REALITY....

It's so real it's like you can become this guy and assimilate with the situations he encounters. We're not talking about a game where you're going to kill a dragon that throws fire at you, that might be fun, but you'll never do that in real life. In this game you will get hungry and you have to sleep, otherwise your eyes will close during an important quest. You can eat spoiled food and die from it. You'll go to jail if they catch you doing something wrong, when you're being jumped by a group, the camera will be all over just like it feels when a few people are using your head as a percussion drum. You'll be put in situations that test your morality and compassion. The fakest thing I found in the game was the "alchemy". 

What a vast world this is..

Once I leveled up and understood the mechanics of the game, I truly enjoyed exploring the vastness of this world. In doing the side quests you learn to hunt, horse ride, improve strength, agility, speech, etc. etc. making your character Henry a super badass outdoor/knight dude. *Don't forget to train with Bernard as much as you can*. I also learned what a "world" is in "video game terms" and the world here is vast and rich. You really have to behave accordingly, i.e. not assault people in the street or steal something in plain view, but trust me, you do get the chance to choke people out, fight them and steal whatever you want, you just can't get caught. There are about 13 cities/locations on the map and they all have their own unique feeling with vendors/traders/armorers/tailors/cobblers that you have to interact and do commerce with. You have to build your wealth. For me, the easiest way was to start fighting enemies, steal their armor, fix it, and sell it around the towns. You also get to DRINK!!, get drunk one night or two and see where you wake up, you never know, you might be far away from home. Play some dice WHILE drunk! ,,, you can go to the taverns and play dice while drinking with the customers there and win all their money. There are caves and silver mines you get to explore and get lost in. The forest/woods area is HUGE. You will find all sorts of things there, you might be walking around and decide to shoot this one rabbit or full grown deer that just appeared next to you, you can skin it and get the hides or get the antlers or teeth, or the meat, you can sell all of this to make your wealth as well but consider that killing game is also considered against the law. But is another way of making your wealth. You will learn to brew your own potions and remedies that will help you in fights (give you more stamina and regenerate health faster). There are "bathhouses where you can pay for a wench and a "good time" any time you want, they can also heal your wounds when you need to heal so keep that in mind. You need to learn how to read, remember that as a blacksmith's son in 1403 you and a lot more people would be illiterate so you need to pick up and develop this skill as well, it will come in handy later on. As you do all these activities, your character keeps leveling up so when you encounter your next enemy, you'll have the upper hand. There are MANY side quests that truly immerse you into exploring all the little niches of the game, I highly suggest that you try an do them all. 

All the locations and characters are real locations and people, well maybe not Henry, but the kings and story of the time is real. Google the cities and you'll find the rich history that this game is based on. Cities like Rattay, Talmberg, Ledetchko, Sasau, Uzhitz, etc... it's all there. Research about King Wenceslas and Sigismund of Hungary.

This game was my introduction to what an "open world" "RPG" game really is, and I can't be more happy with my decision to continue the game when I had my doubts about it. I finished this with 182 hours of game time and I know I left parts of the world unexplored. I really love this world, I love Henry and his journey, I love the time that this game is based on and I love the attention to detail that WarHorse put in developing this game.

To sum up, this game is DEF worth your time, def worth my 182 hours so far on it. I really enjoyed it and look forward to more hours exploring the DLC's and more of the world. But don't take my word for it, try it yourself..

I finally had the time to beat this game in big 2025 and I'm so glad I chose to go on this adventure. The friction in its systems encourage you to engage with a world that has no magic with such sincerity, I would have never expected it. The Elder Scrolls isn't coming back any time soon, but I think we might have found something better.

Kingdom Come Deliverance is the only game I have ever played that i have officially dubbed:
"Realistic Medieval Life Simulator RPG". Firstly, the game is great, regardless of what anyone else says about bugs and combat being impossible. (I'll address this in a moment.) 

Now before jumping to conclusions, no, this isnt skyrim, no you are not the dragonborn, nor are you the destined hero, or the prodigy warrior.

you're a peasant named Henry. Now put yourself in Henry's shoes, a mid-twenties 14th century villager with no combat or life experience other that MAYBE helping his dad forge swords from time to time, otherwise he's a drunk who plays pranks, and enjoys life. Suddenly shit hits the fan when a major event unfolds.

You are cast into a world, with no experience, no gear, no remorse, and no one gives a damn about you and your problems. Now, that is to say, you won't be useless forever, everything takes time and effort, and if you're really committed you can learn how to become better at combat, better at protecting yourself, better at archery, and so on.

just remember to ask yourself these questions: 
- What would Henry do?
- Will doing THIS piss off that person? (if you have to ask, yes, yes it will.)
- No, people do not leave their belongings scattered around to loot at your own free will. Will I become a thief? where can i learn to pick a lock? stealth? pickpocketing? you need to LEARN.
- Would i be able to survive a fight against 3 Bandits when the only thing i know about a sword is where the point end goes? Take it a step further, could I (That's you) fight 3 grown ass adults with at least 10 years of combat experience in a dark alley in RL?

Eventually, you'll just be a god knight cleaving your way through hordes of enemies and me a master at everything, but like everything, becoming a master takes time. Pace yourself, and BE HENRY, learn, play, adapt, and triumph.

I don't write many reviews but after playing this game i felt compelled to do so. I tend not to buy games at release, knowing they will be full of bugs and I waited 9 months to buy this, despite having seen trailers and being very excited for it. I'm glad that I did. From what i have read and seen, at release there were a number of bugs which were either extremely immersion breaking or critically game breaking. Happily i can say that they seem to be fixed. Let me say first, for those of you on the fence considering buying this game because you love RPG's and think you may enjoy it but have been scared off by reviews or videos, like I was... Ignore all of it. Buy the game. It is simply incerdible. I have been a fan of RPG's all of my (32 year long) life and I can honestly say that this is among my favourite RPG experiences ever. I have played most huge titles such as Final Fantasy, Diablo, Elder Scrolls, Witcher, Fallout, Dragon Age, Mass Effect, Deus Ex, Baldurs Gate.. the list could go on, but i have rarely been so abosrbed by a game as this. The world Warhorse have created is exceptional, especially for a first time effort. Bethesda should take notice here.... True, it took me maybe 5-10 hours to get used to the mechanics and start to be able to truly appreciate what they have created but i think that is how any good RPG should be.
This is quite simply a masterpiece. I cannot put into words how good it is, it has to be played to truly understand. 
The world Warhorse have created in arguably the most alive i have seen in any game ever, period. Everything you do has significance in the grand scheme of the plot. Each interaction with the dynamic populous has potentially far reaching consequences. Combat, although harsh at the beginning and frustrating at times is incredibly well executued. I live in England and feel sometimes when riding out in the wild that i am simply taking a stroll in the local woods. it is ucanny how accurately they have portrayed the environment. Yes, it fails to teach you a lot in the beginning and yes it can be difficult to get to grips with the huge amount of systems required to play effectively but give it time and there will come a point where it clicks... and when it does, you will come to understand that you are playing a game that may be a genre defining title, destined to go down in history. For me, the quality of immersion in a game has to do with the suspension of disbelief, the same as it does in a movie or book. It is measured against the player's feeling of involvement in the story and the atmosphere of the game world. In Kingdom Come: Deliverance, these attributes coincide in a way that they rarely do in any medium. Slogging through the mud in the driving rain, barely alive after a battle with my vision clouded by blood, never felt so real and immediate. This game was built to be involving and, in that regard, is an absolute triumph. For anyone who likes a good RPG and is even a little interested in medieval times, Kingdom Come: Deliverance is a must. A game that could give any Elder Scrolls title a run for it's money.

Please note: This is a HARDCORE RPG EXPERIENCE. It may be similar, but it does not play like Skyrim. Expect a steep learning curve in areas like combat, stealth, lockpicking, and alchemy especially.

TO ADDRESS THE BIGGEST ISSUE PEOPLE BRING UP: Yes, this game has it's fair share of bugs, and I do put a lot on the heads of Warhorse for many of them still not being fixed. THAT BEING SAID, Warhorse is not Bethesda. It is a much smaller studio that doesn't employ nearly as many people. It's expected for it to take longer for them to roll out fixes.

ABOUT THE GAME:
As I mentioned before, KCD is a hardcore RPG experience. You have a set character. There are third party appearance mods out there, but suffice to say you will be playing a male character, Henry, son of a Blacksmith. The game is historically accurate to an appropriate level that doesn't hinder the gameplay.

Combat-wise, this game may be difficult to get into, but once you learn the system, you'll find it greatly rewarding. The system is almost similar to For Honor. You have different attack and parry angles, combos, etc to use. There's a variety of weapon types and playstyle differences. Want to be a ranger, going around sniping people with a bow? You do you, boo. I personally play a longswordsman. Longsword and shield don't mesh well together, so if you'd prefer a classic shield and sword, remember short swords, maces, and hand axes are your friends.

Skill-wise, this game differs drastically from the Elder Scrolls series as well. Alchemy is done at an alchemist table, much like Skyrim, but requires precise mechanics, and isn't simply mixing a couple things together to create a potion. You need to stoke the flames, time how long ingredients cook, choose your base, grind certain herbs, and follow very precise recipes that don't reward failure. But once you master it, alchemy is your greatest Ally.
Stealth is it's own beast as well. Every single layer of armor (there are multiple, and all armor stacks into different layers you can equip) has it's own weight, shine that affects visibility, amount of noise it generates, etc. So stealth is a factor of many different variables and can also be difficult to master. Pickpocketing and lockpicking are their own minigames. It's not simply rummaging in someone's pocket. A game of skill is involved with it, rather than a percentage-based success rate. You can still succeed while being absolute shit in it stat-wise. Same goes for lockpicking.

Overall, this game is a stat-oriented RPG experience that plays off some of the best aspects of The Elder Scrolls series. For many, it has it's drawbacks. The hardcore RPG factor could be a turnoff for some, However, the experience can be greatly rewarding for those who invest the time. The game has a modding scene found of Nexusmods, and many of them can be invaluable. I recommend checking some of them out for a better experience, especially if you're a more casual player. I originally discovered this game when Nerdcubed, a man who usually hates RPGs, found this game and loved it. Since I have picked it up, I have enjoyed it greatly, and believe any fan of more hardcore RPG experiences, and any fan of Elder Scrolls titles will enjoy this game as well. Give it a look, and remember, this is a smaller studio behind this game. Give it some patience, and save often with the Unlimited Saving mod.

One of the best open-world RPGs I've ever played. I understand some people might disagree, but here is my short review on why this game is worth your time (contains spoilers for the prologue):

Widely considered one of the most accurate and realistic medieval settings ever created in gaming. Now, don't get me wrong, it is still a work of fiction, but the portrayal of real geographical locations and politics is well-placed. If you want to play an RPG without any fantasy elements, this is as close as you can get.

The story and the characters go well with the setting. There is no grand scheme where the protagonist is needed to save the world; there's just politics. Henry (the protagonist) was just an ordinary guy in his early 20s until an army razed his village to take the silver mines. After losing everything, our protagonist here acts recklessly, which is natural for a human being with that much trauma. I love how the prologue ends and the game actually starts when Henry gets his shit together and starts his new life in Rattay. The prologue might teach you a bit about the game, like the basics of combat, but this is normally the point when you actually start leveling and progressing your in-game skills.

That brings me to the next points: combat and progression. The combat is responsible for some negative reviews out there, and I think it's fair. Some might call it janky or downright terrible, and I understand if they feel that way. I can respect that. But, I'd like to invite you to take your time and get used to how combat works in this game, because you might end up enjoying it just like I do. That said, the combat is unique, unlike most video games where they give your character a sword and they immediately move like it's an extension of their arm. I have hundreds of hours in Soulsborne games, but even the combat difficulty in this game is different. I'm not saying it's harder; I'm saying it is different. Hence, why it needs a different approach to master.

At first, Henry swings a sword like it weighs 100lbs. Combined with me fighting like I was playing Skyrim, I was easily killed by a mere 3 peasants. Practicing with Captain Bernard until your sword skill reaches level 5 and learning the "master strike" will make the combat far more forgiving. Even with that, you should think twice before fighting multiple armed men jumping you in the forest. It is possible to win that kind of fight at some point, but you should also think if it's worth risking your life for. That's what the game is trying to tell you. Don't fight like you're chosen by destiny; fight like you're just a man in medieval times with everything to lose.

Progression of other skills is also satisfying to master. Level up your speech skill and become Henry of Gaslitz, inventor of gaslighting. Then the guards will think twice before accusing you of a murder that they witnessed right before their eyes. Go to Uzhitz, find the scribe, ask him to teach Henry how to read, and continue leveling the skill. It'll benefit you a lot and even ease some quests.

Overall, it's an incredible game. You don't have to take my word for it; it would be better for you to try it out yourself and see if you like it or not. $5.99 (on sale) for this is a great deal.

Maybe the best role-playing game I've ever played. By far the most interesting and realistic take to a medieval setting I've seen, from a time period and country, often overlooked which it provides enough background to get a feel of whats going down.

On the subject of the main character, I think that Henry might be one of my new favorite video game protagonists of all time. His reactions and mannerisms to mistakes and events in the game were, most of the time, overlapping with my own reactions to different things. A solid "what the fuck?" is all a character really needs to express his disbelief to a surprising event, and I think the game does a solid job at making sure his reactions are believable and measured.

For side/minor characters voice acting is all pretty good with a couple standout performances and memorable lines (see Sir Hanush). Models are often reused for minor characters, which is pretty noticeable, but they're high enough quality to give it a slide.

For gameplay and combat I can wholeheartedly say that there is nothing quite like this game when it comes to medieval combat, with most mechanics being completely original as far as I can tell. This may be the only game that actually has clinching in a sword-fight, even if it isn't really all that in depth. All the weapons and combos feel pretty damn good and maybe the one spot where weaponry is lacking is the pole-arms, which are unable to be carried in your inventory, for they are extremely hard to get in on when an enemy has one and seem to not have any combos or anything for them to be used with.

Progression for the combat is very satisfying and once you get past the early game slog, learning perfect-parries and combos will swiftly lead you to becoming a master-class swordsman. Early game its maybe a little too difficult to compete with the enemy AI because you won't be able to perfect-parry and normal blocks are practically worthless, but once you get over that hump and get some good armor you will be perfectly capable of one-man-armying groups of like 6 or 7 people in camps without dying. The combat becomes maybe a little too reliant on perfect-parries when enemies outnumber you by a large number since you won't have the opportunity to get combos off when you're being swarmed. One of the only big issues with the combat is when the enemies have dogs, because they will run at you and lock you in place by biting your arm, leaving you completely at the mercy of the enemies.

It's about time I put together a review of this masterpiece.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance is, hands down, the best modern true RPG I've played in the past decade. No other game comes close. But, before I get into the reasons why that's the case, let me make one thing clear: This game IS NOT Skyrim. It is NOT the Witcher 3. 

Those are fantastic games but if that's what you want here, you will 100%, unequivocally be disappointed. Simply look at the Steam discussions for this game for countless examples of that. The devs have always been perfectly clear about what this game was going to be. 

If you choose not to do your due diligence and buy into this game just because it looks like Skyrim, that's on you - not us and not the devs. Refund the game and move on. This game is closer to a classic RPG than anything else. Its mechanics are complex, its gameplay is realistic, and the world has a high level of reactivity that you only find in the likes of Baldur's Gate and the early Fallout games.

I also want to be clear that I'm not of the opinion (As some are) that I'm some sort of "hardcore" amazing gamurrrr and that I'm somehow superior to everyone that doesn't like this game. I'm simply part of a niche audience that this game was targeted at - all I'm saying is, if you're not also a part of that niche audience, this game is not for you. Please bear that in mind as you read my review.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]

Kingdom Come: Deliverance is a pretty game. Aside from some odd-looking faces here and there (take it from someone learning 3D modeling - creating faces is HARD), the graphics are gorgeous and realistic. Forests are incredibly dense, much more than you'd ever see with something like Skyrim. If you don't look at your map, you can truly get lost in them, especially at night. Animations are, for the most part also very good.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

This game is realistic. If that word turns you off, buy something else. Otherwise, read on. 
Players must manage hunger and fatigue, with drawbacks for ignoring both (no lethal ones, as far as I know), but these aren't annoying like they can be in a survival game. They are side mechanics that never intrude too much unless you really ignore them. If you do, Henry (the main character) will start to have his vision impacted (it blurs and his eyes drift shut briefly every few seconds). 

As previously stated, reactivity is important. Depending on how you behave, how you look, even how you smell, the world will treat you differently. Trying to persuade a peasant to trust you? Wear ratty, dirty clothes and don't bathe. Trying to suck up to a noble? Wear fancy clothes, freshly laundered. There was actually one instance where I looked so terrifying that a bandit who mugged me while fast traveling instantly surrendered when I dismounted and pulled my sword out.

Both you and your enemies can surrender if a fight stops going your way - very few enemies will be bloodthirsty enough to kill you. However, you and they can demand something in return for this. When you interact with a surrendering enemy (if you are distracted fighting their pal, they may try to run away) you can let them go with their weapons intact, demand payment for their release, let them go but disarm them, or continue the fight and kill them. 

Additionally, you don't have to kill anybody in the game, as far as I'm aware (some bosses may be an exception, but I can't confirm that as I haven't even gotten that far). Simply equip a blunt weapon and knock them out if you so choose. In fact, I believe it's possible to completely avoid combat the vast majority of the time. 

[h1]Gameplay, Part Deux[/h1]

The game's skill system is also realistic. Henry starts by being horrible at everything, in true RPG fashion. I say "true RPG" because the game puts an emphasis on character skills over personal player skills. 

This distinction is important - one says "I can be good at everything because I have good mouse aim" while the other says "You're going to suck at everything because your character sucks at everything".

At the start, your bow aim will be wobbly and inaccurate. Lockpicking will be extremely difficult. Pickpocketing will be nearly impossible. If you fail, you must live with the consequences due to the game's save system. 

You are not allowed to save scum. There are no manual saves unless you purchase an expensive alcoholic beverage (alcohol has its own serious drawbacks unless you put perk points into your "drinking" skill) or sleep in a bed. That's it. Otherwise, it's all autosaves. 

Now, upon launch, there were some issues with this system. For instance, if you need to quit the game because you're pressed for time, you'd lose your progress since the last autosave or manual save. However, the devs are implementing a system that will fix this - when you leave, the game saves, and you can reload that save once you come back. But then the save is deleted, so you can't savescum. If you don't like the sound of the save system (with this new feature included), do not buy this game. You will hate it.

[h1]RPG Mechanics[/h1]

I briefly delved into the skill system earlier, but I'll elaborate on it here. As I said, you suck at everything to start with. The only way to improve is to try things or visit a trainer but the latter only get you so far - you must fill in the skill gaps between training sessions yourself. Want to improve your speech? 

Try using one of the many bluff options on people (Usually, there's 3 - intimidate, persuade and one other that I'm not sure about, the symbol is weird). If you fail and things go south, again, live with it and move on. You get experience and improve whether you fail or succeed. 

Same goes for lockpicking and other skills. You learn by doing. You can likely eventually become a "master of everything" like you can in Skyrim, but it'll take a long time and your best bet is to stick to a character archetype that suits your playstyle. 

Aside from regular skills (which are composed of Alchemy, Drinking, Herbalism, Horsemanship, Hunting, Lockpicking, Maintenance, Pickpocketing, Reading and Stealth), you also have combat skills and stats to worry about.  

All of these skills and stats have perks that go with them. These perks unlock additional abilities and traits, both major and minor. A lot of them come with drawbacks - for example, the "Beer Bibber" trait gets you drunk 50% slower from beer, but wine is twice as strong. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

It seems I'm running out of characters, so I guess I'll have to end it here - it's funny because I could easily go on for thousands more words and still not cover everything this game has to offer. 

At any rate, if you like the sound of the game from what I've said so far, buy it! Prove to the devs this sort of game still has an audience.

Early in the main quest of KCD, I came across two ragged, starving bandits whom I had to fight against. Looking back now -with hundreds of hours played since, those two enemies are laughably weak. But at the time, due to my inexperience with the game and my character's lack of levels, it meant that I was in for the fight of my life! 

An intense, harrowing struggle ensued, rivaling any soul-shattering boss battle I had played in games prior. After what felt like an eternity, I manged to overcome the two brigands by a razor's edge. The battle had left my character bleeding, with tattered clothes, cracked armor, and a chipped, dulled blade no longer capable of effectively cutting. The experience was exhausting, exhilarating, and ultimately immensely satisfying -and I think this small anecdotal story accurately symbolizes Kingdom Come: Deliverance as a whole.

The game is beautiful, imaginative, and brutal. It's an action adventure RPG fused with survival mechanics and hyper-grounded in realism. 

One of the biggest facets of the game that stood out to me was the immersion. The creators put in much attention to detail and it shows. Almost every every NPC can be interacted with in some way -and they respond to the player's behavior (good or bad) and reputation. The landscape of 1400s Bohemia is beautiful, inviting, and forbidding, with rolling grass covered hills, winding rivers and streams, expansive farmland enclosures, thick dark forests, deep craggy defiles, and ruins of ill-fated villages and towns. In between the major population centers of the game are plenty of points of interest including treasure, various camps, scenes of tragic accidents, random encounters, and hunting and fishing locations. 

The combat -while it can be challenging (and comes with a bit of a learning curve) is very satisfying. It requires a proper grasp of timing, distance management, and correct inputs in order to be successful. The direction of your attacks are input-based, crucial for feinting, doing combos, and striking at the least armored regions of your opponents. In addition, a number of the techniques and animations have a historical basis, being taken from 15th century combat manuscripts. If anything, this shows just how committed the creators were to the grounded realism aspect of the game. There are plenty of weapons and weapon types to choose from, all with their own unique strengths and weaknesses depending on the situation. Armor plays a key part of combat as well, and unlike most other games, where armor simply acts as part of the players' "skin" -reducing damage taken by a % amount, in KCD armor actually prevents you (and your allies/enemies) from taking damage from attacks. 

That said, the game offers far more than just fun combat. There are extensive stealth mechanics, as well as criminality (and quest lines to go along with such a playstyle), dialogue-based avenues for handling quests, alchemy, horseback riding, trading and haggling, gambling, cooking, hunting, and exploring. Every single skill in the game takes time to level up and improve, which -while slightly time consuming, only adds to the feeling a accomplishment once you master said skill.

KCD is very well voice-acted and mo-capped, from the most irrelevant NPC found in the farthest backwater, to the integral pieces of the main plot, to the main character himself, Henry of Skalitz. The game's strict adherence to being as grounded as possible means that every character talks and acts like it's Bohemia 1403 AD. This means you won't have anachronisms with people talking like it's 2021 in a medieval setting (*cough* Ubisoft, Assassin's Creed *cough*)

The overall narrative and main plot is interesting and serviceable, acting more like a window into the world that is Kingdom Come: Deliverance rather than the carrying force behind the game. The real sell is the fun but challenging combat and the loads of immersive features that accompany a creative vision like KCD. 

It's a great and memorable journey, and I was not disappointed at any point. I understand that back during the game's initial release there were some issues with bugs, but during my hundreds of hours in-game I've rarely come across any serious issues. Usually, if there is a bug, it comes of the form of very temporary and benign sound glitches.

Ultimately, I put KCD in my pantheon of best games. 10/10. Period, end of story. If you have the time and patience to put the effort in, the game is incredibly rewarding. But now I have to go, because I feel quite hungry....

It's a masterpiece. 

What you get when you buy this game is an entry into a medieval world. The developers have attempted to create an authentic experience of 15th-century Bohemia, and for me, it works.

You'll wander a beautifully crafted, richly detailed, lush summer landscape, along mud roads and footpaths, through villages, pastures, farmsteads, small towns, silver mines and forests. You will see the castles and mansions of nobility, the dwellings of town burghers, the farmers' houses and barns, the hovels of the charcoal burners and woodcutters, and the camps of mercenaries and refugees. You'll witness various craftsmen and agriculturalists at work with contemporary tools and methods; you'll visit a church construction site and see medieval architecture, scaffolding and stonecutting; you will talk to the hangman, the cobbler, the preacher, the huntsman, the itinerant knight, the nobleman and the carpenter; you will court the noble lady and the miller's wench; you will hear about kings Wenceslas and Sigismund, about a certain preacher named Jan Hus, and people called Waldensians; you will learn about the difficulties of medieval rulers and succession, about counterfeit coins and unruly nobles. You will join a cloister and experience the arduous daily routine of the Benedictine monks; you will fight and brawl, eat, sleep, pick flowers, sneak into bandit camps at night, grind swords, run errands and solve crimes.

There are almost none of the tropes you find in modern fantasy movies. Castles are not giant skyscrapers of stone, but essentially fortified mansions, defended by a few dozen men. War is not glorious battles between huge perfectly uniformed armies marching in step; instead, there are raids by bands of unruly mercenaries who compensate for their lack of pay with plunder and violating women. Of course, the story contains some Hollywood clichés, of course sometimes the characters act and speak probably more like 21st-century Americans than 15th-century Bohemians. But none of them have blue dreadlocks or bodybuilder muscles. And among the soldiers there are no model-sized women in steel armour bikinis. 

There is steel armour though, and lots of it. But it is usually dirty, as you will be, if you don't visit the bath-houses regularly. 

This game paints an incredibly detailed, endlessly colourful (that includes dirt, rain and mud) portrayal of medieval Europe the like of which I have never seen in a game. The amount of research the developers must have done is staggering. How did a medieval beehive look, or a tanner's workshop? What were the roots and outcomes of the conflict between Wenceslas and Sigismund, and what the contentions of church reformers/heretics? What did monks do all day, and for which reasons did they join a cloister? Why was a siege difficult? How might a lord act whose birthright and duty it is to rule, but whose inclination is to hunt, play and drink? ...

Unfortunately, Bohemia in 1403 was not quite as "diverse" (=non-white) as progressive activists want to paint it. There are, of course, the Cumans - a Turkic warrior people -  who play an important role, but they are not black. Consequently, the developers were accused of racism, right-wing propaganda, etc. by people who believe it is the foremost duty of game designers to spread progressive ideas of "diversity" and "inclusion".

But believe it or not, games can foster sympathy for minorities even without ideologues doing the storywriting. There is a homosexual character in the game whom you encounter briefly. He is not a bad or incompetent person, but he lives in a world in which everyone believes (including himself) that homosexuality is an abomination. He therefore feels guilty and avoids any contact to the others who either don't know about him or detest him for something that he has no power over. He tries to atone by working hard. That is an authentic way a homosexual might have experienced life in 1403, and there is deep individual tragedy in that.

Kingdom Come made me scream in anger as often as it made me gape in awe. Difficulty can be punishing at times. The save system is as strict as the Benedictine rule. Bugs and crashes plague the player as the smallpox did Bohemian peasantry. The innovative combat system is marred by a terrible quick-time mechanic which completely devalues technique or finesse. But this game is a jewel. It's a feast for the eyes, the ears and the heart. Its scope, its ambition, its immersion are second to none for me.

It's a unique game, something different from the dopamine-optimized high-octane fast action gameplay that has become the standard for "non-cozy" games. Kingdom Come: Deliverance is slow and clunky, but has an incredible charm and large, large focus on the role-playing aspect of the RPG. For me, the game draws many similarities to games like Skyrim, but this game is better in practically every way. Characters in KCD feel very real and the main story is compelling enough to keep me interested. And while the combat in this game is EXTREMELY flawed, it adequately portrays a story in itself as you, playing Henry of Skalitz, go from someone who struggles to take down a single person to a fearsome knight capable of slaying multiple men at once.

The way the combat evolves alongside your knowledge and understanding of how it works is a double-edged sword. The "Master-Parry" system essentially guarantees that you can succeed in any swordfight by playing like a coward and never swinging first. Additionally, because enemies can ALSO master parry you, you're punished for fighting offensively on more skilled enemies, with no course of action to avoid getting hit other than to simply not ever swing first. As you progress through the game, this becomes less of an issue in random encounters due to your overwhelming stat advantage, but more of an issue in late-game quests involving fights with higher-difficulty enemies. Over the course of my playtime, I fell in and out of love with the combat, and recognized how unique and fun it felt to master while also seeing the cracks in the system.

Outside of combat, KCD is extrordinarily slow. You're forced in an animation to pick flowers. You're forced in an animation to open every single door in the entire game. You're forced to stop playing the game constantly in very small but extremely prevalent micro-doses of time. Washing your armor, Waiting for time to pass, Getting in and out of bed, it all takes a small but unnecessary amount of time. This enhances the gritty 1400's medieval RPG aspect of the game to an immense degree, but also comes at the cost of potentially alienating a large audience of people who simply don't have the time or patience to play the game. Combined with the functional but outdated U.I. of the inventory and skills screens, I put down this game in the tutorial area two individual times before I was finally in the right mindset to play it through on my third.

Despite what may seem like me complaining, I think that Kingdom Come: Deliverance is actually a good game. It's unique and interesting, and if you're both a patient person and also looking for a medieval RPG that stays grounded and real, there isn't a better game on the market for you. I'm only that type of person in periodic bursts of time in my life, so I never managed to finish the game. But I do respect it for what it is, and thoroughly enjoyed a lot of the time I spent playing it while I had the right mindset to do so.

Why Kingdom Come: Deliverance is a Great Game
One of the most defining aspects of Kingdom Come: Deliverance is its dedication to historical accuracy. The game is set in Bohemia during the Middle Ages and eschews the magic and myth of fantasy RPGs for a grounded portrayal of life in the 1400s. Warhorse Studios conducted extensive research to recreate landscapes, towns, and castles as authentically as possible. The architecture, clothing, weaponry, and even social dynamics reflect what life would have been like in that era. This commitment to realism draws players into a world that feels tangible and alive, offering an immersive experience not often found in other RPGs.

Players can explore vibrant forests, towns bustling with daily activity, and the stunning, rolling countryside of Bohemia, all meticulously crafted to match the historical records of the time. By prioritizing historical immersion, Kingdom Come offers an educational yet thrilling experience, making it appealing to both history buffs and casual gamers alike.


Unlike any other game the combat system in Kingdom Come: Deliverance sets it apart from other RPGs. Inspired by real-life medieval fighting techniques, it’s designed to be challenging and rewarding for players who invest time in mastering it. Unlike many games where combat relies on repetitive button-mashing, Kingdom Come requires precision, timing, and tactical thinking. Players can target specific parts of an enemy’s body and must manage stamina, armor weight, and positioning to gain the upper hand in combat.

Additionally, the game’s weapon system emphasizes realism. Swords, maces, and other weapons have specific strengths and weaknesses depending on an opponent’s armor, making the choice of weapon and approach a strategic consideration. This complex system enhances the sense of accomplishment, as players genuinely improve over time. The difficulty and depth of the combat reflect the brutal reality of medieval warfare and lend authenticity to the gameplay experience.

3. Character Development and Moral Complexity
Unlike many RPGs that give players the power to create and shape their character from scratch, Kingdom Come puts players in the role of Henry, a blacksmith’s son seeking revenge and purpose after his village is destroyed by a foreign invasion. Henry starts as a relatively inexperienced character, mirroring the average person rather than a born hero, which makes his journey all the more relatable and rewarding.

Henry’s moral choices are rarely black and white, allowing players to explore a morally ambiguous world where decisions have lasting consequences. Side quests and interactions often challenge players to think critically about ethics and survival, especially in a time when justice was far from fair or forgiving. This depth in character and decision-making strengthens the narrative, giving players a complex, immersive experience that feels both personal and meaningful.

4. Detailed Progression System and Realistic Survival Elements
In Kingdom Come: Deliverance, skills don’t improve simply by leveling up; they require practice. For instance, if Henry wants to become a better swordsman, he must train with his sword. This grounded approach to character progression makes each achievement feel earned. Players learn from mistakes, building Henry’s skills and knowledge as they encounter the various challenges of medieval life.

The game also introduces survival elements, adding layers of realism to Henry’s journey. Players must manage hunger, exhaustion, and hygiene, making choices that directly affect Henry’s health, stamina, and reputation. These survival mechanics don’t feel intrusive; rather, they deepen the experience by immersing players in the daily hardships and decisions faced by people in the medieval period. Eating, resting, and even maintaining one’s armor are essential aspects of staying alive and being effective in combat, adding to the game’s realism.

5. Innovative Storytelling and Quest Design
While many RPGs follow a straightforward quest structure, Kingdom Come: Deliverance offers players dynamic and open-ended missions that can be completed in a variety of ways. Players are given choices not just in dialogue but also in how they approach situations. This flexibility allows for creativity in solving problems, whether through diplomacy, stealth, or brute force.

The main storyline is compelling, with plenty of emotional stakes, and the side quests are just as engaging. Side quests are not simple filler; they offer intricate narratives, unique challenges, and insights into the characters and world of Bohemia. The choices players make in these quests can have ripple effects throughout the game, creating a world where actions truly matter.

6. An Appreciation for Patience and Thoughtful Gameplay
Kingdom Come: Deliverance is not a game for players looking for fast-paced, action-heavy gameplay. It rewards patience, strategic thinking, and careful planning. Whether learning the ins and outs of sword fighting, navigating intricate dialogues, or finding one’s way through the dense forests of Bohemia, players are rewarded for their attentiveness and problem-solving skills. The slower pace invites players to savor the details and become fully immersed in the world. For players who appreciate a slower, more deliberate RPG experience, Kingdom Come is a rare gem that delivers a deeply satisfying adventure.

Conclusion
In an era where many RPGs rely on fantastical elements to engage players, Kingdom Come: Deliverance offers a refreshing, historically grounded experience. With its intricate combat system, richly detailed world, complex storytelling, and realistic survival mechanics, the game sets a new standard for immersion in the RPG genre. By prioritizing realism and depth over convenience and spectacle, Warhorse Studios has created a game that encourages players to step back in time and experience the world as it was, not as we might wish it to be. For players who crave a challenging and authentic RPG, Kingdom Come: Deliverance is an exceptional choice that stands out for its commitment to delivering a truly immersive, thoughtful gaming experience.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance is an adventure game focused on immersing you in the late medieval European countryside. I don’t regret the time I spent with it.

For me, the main obstacle to enjoying it was the myriad of labels this game carries. You might hear that it’s an RPG, open-world, survival, historical, or hardcore game. All of that is kind of true, but if you come in expecting any of those elements to shine, you’ll be disappointed. Character progression and choice/consequence in this game are rudimentary. The open world is deliberately functional and far from the tradition of an interactive, varied map. Survival elements might scare you at first, but once you get familiar with the game, they stop being an issue. The historical accuracy sits somewhere below an Assassin’s Creed game (no sci-fi elements though, aside from Easter eggs) and above your average Hollywood historical epic. The supposed “hardcoreness” is mostly smoke and mirrors.

Going into this with preconceived notions, I saw a harsh beginning and thought it was a typical Eurojank experience: a hardcore, completionist-type game where you have to do every side quest and explore every patch of land just to stand a chance. But it’s not that at all. It’s actually a very casual, handholding game. Every element I listed is kind of weak on its own, but all of them exist to create an immersive experience. You have hunger and energy meters, but they’re only a problem early on, before you understand how everything works. Later, they just set a rhythm for your adventure, reminding you when it’s time to find a tavern, eat, and sleep. You start poor and weak, but if you just follow the main story for a while, you’ll be trained and equipped to handle anything. Then you just travel the land, help people, and do chores. The vast majority of tasks don’t involve combat or have peaceful resolutions, and the combat itself is clunky, it mostly happens to you on your way somewhere.

It may sound like I don’t think the game is good, but I respect what it does: it puts you in a historical setting and doesn’t try to fill the map with distractions out of fear you’ll be bored. This game takes pride in letting you be bored. The map still feels condensed, but it’s empty enough to feel authentic at the same time. Its version of history is idealized, sanitized, and inconsistent, but it still offers more authenticity and immersion than most games do, and I appreciate what I experienced here.

Definitely try it if the idea of riding a horse across the rural countryside for three minutes without seeing anything interesting sounds like a good time to you.

A flawed game, but a marvelous experience in a medieval world and a welcome break from all the fantasy, dragon slaying, save the world shenanigans that populate the recent RPG revival. It's really a unique experience and a "from zero to hero" textbook story. It occasionally suffers from Skyrim levels of NPC incompetence, which is slightly off-putting, but hey, we'll excuse the nobles for ordering you around. Even after you've built a trebuchet, acquired enough stone to build St. Vitus' Cathedral 526 years earlier, slain and skinned enough animals to feed a medieval Woodstock and then proceeded to single-handedly liberate their entire castle. And sleep with their wife. But, shhhh, don't tell them that.

Some wonky mechanics coupled with a rigorous and drunk saving system which only allows you to save if you swig a schnapps (it autosaves at certain points and when sleeping), often make this as frustrating as it is awe inspiring. The skills increase the more you use them and you basically start as a complete wimp. Don't even try attacking a tree, negotiating a better price or brewing a potion. You'll get beaten to a pulp, kicked out of a store and poison yourself. Training is everything. Certain levels also grant you perk points that you can save for later or use for already unlocked perks. Combat has a very significant learning curve and is painfully punishing until you train your skills with wooden weapons. It's all about patience, proper timing and paying attention to the movements of your enemies. Unless you're outnumbered. Then it's time to run and practice your close-up archery snapshots of their faces. Or just yell and whistle for Pebbles (your one and only horse, there will never be others) and canter away through the lush Bohemian forests. 

Combat simulates injuries and bleeding, shakes when you get hit, usually disorienting you, has 5 sides from which you can attack and block, takes into account what kind of weapon you're wielding against what armor, if you're using a shield or a two-handed weapon, if you're drunk, tired, overeaten, how many wenches you've slept with, how damaged your armor and weapon are, are you wearing a white padded shirt or a black one, are your pants chaffing you and is your coif strap stuck in your beard. It's complicated. And oh so satisfying getting the hang of it and defeating 3 or even more enemies in a straight up sword fight. Even more satisfying when you sneak up on a camp at night and silently put everyone out of their daily misery of washing their breeches in the same pond their companion emptied his bowels into a few hours earlier. This is where those wonky mechanics and restrictions really help with the feeling of realism.

The world is very detailed, thoroughly researched, beatiful, realistic, populated with believable historical touches and kept to a small scale which just elevates everything to a whole new level. A simple horse ride through the forest at night, only a torch in hand or a hunting trip just exude atmosphere and being in the middle of the forest really feels like great woodland. You can run into farms, grave markers, random points of interest, accidents and even ambushes. There's no loading screens in the world. There's also no fast travel in a "beam me up, Scotty" way. Time passes when you fast travel and you can see yourself on the map. Visits to the cities really feel like populated, breathing, living medieval cities with people sleeping, washing, bringing water in the early morning, eating, gambling, begging and having their daily routines. You should probably also do some of those things unless you want to be a dirty, mud-caked, ragged, drunk insomniac. At least do it for the ladies in the "bathhouses". People also react to you differently depending how dirty you are, what clothes you're wearing and how your reputation stands.

The survival mechanics are much gentler than what I expected and don't really present a problem in a normal game, but still give you something to watch out for unlike most other survival games where you're just perpetually hungry and need to eat 2 cows to make it through a day.

The main questline and story are solid. Nothing spectacular, but competently written with believable characters, good twists and nice set pieces. Henry is a loveable buffoon with dubious powers of decision making and a penchant for trouble, but is a great character. All the main protagonists are marvelously written and voiced, Theresa being my absolute favorite. I really like the mass combat set ups from the main story. They're loud, chaotic, frenzied and dirty, like they probably really were in medieval times. Side quests are great, plentiful, some are really funny, others punch you in the feels and some are outright magical, but without fireballs.

The game still stutters here and there on my setup, but nothing major. I've seen a few more issues, even after all the patches. Guards overlapping on the same spot like some two-headed abominations, texture popping and weird animation glitches. But who knows how people really saw the world in medieval times? It might be historically accurate.

There are two jarring things in KCD and I know most people won't be on my side for this one. Fantasy teleporting horses and fantasy "bag of holding my entire castle" chests. I know both things are there for player convenience, but in a game doing it's utmost to be as realistic as possible, without exact map markers, rough and tough combat and tons of menial things you need to do, those two fantasy elements really poke me in the eye. Perhaps Warhorse Studios should have been a bit more brave, clamped on this and upped the realism even more, forgetting the convenience. There is a little thing called Hardcore mode, with mandatory negative perks, a lot of changes, no compass, no combat indicators, deadlier combat and a lot of other delightful improvements to make your playthrough as close to living hell as possible. Horses still teleport.

Most of the mechanics can be improved with mods and there's a bunch of great ones over on Nexusmods. Even the drunk saving mechanic can be made into a save anywhere/anytime thing, but that would definitely diminish the feeling of accomplishment you get from the game, at least for the first playthrough. That experience needs to be lived through.

There are 4 story DLC's that add a lot more play time. A Woman's Lot puts you in the shoes of Theresa and is my personal favorite, followed by The Amorous Adventures of Bold Sir Hans Capon. The other two are ok as DLC's go.

KCD can and will occupy a lot of your time, but ultimately seems to be an acquired taste. If you're partial to "normal" RPGs and can't bear through some "hardcore" mechanics, KCD is probably not for you. If you're sour with the oversaturated taste of samey fantasy RPGs and can grit your teeth like a true medieval serf getting a whipping from your lord, give KCD a spin.

It's hard to find medieval open world games that don't include (dark) fantasy themes, that's why Kingdom Come: Deliverance is really a one of a kind game and for many a dream come true. The game director is Daniel Vávra, which some of you may recognize for his previous work on Mafia. While Mafia tried to realistically depict mob life, Kingdom Come tries to depict Bohemia's medieval life. As usual, the story is interesting, with well-written dialogues and characters performing greatly. Although there is only one ending, there are multiple choices that affect how you get to the final outcome and how other characters react to your actions.

The quests design is very good. There are countless of quests with really great variation of content and level of freedom. Some side quests are even linked to main quests, but they can only be completed prior to the main quests conclusion. There are also many "fetch quests" (go there and get this item for me), but they are all properly contextualized with texts or dialogues and never a simple copy/past. Generally, side quests give you more freedom than main quests, allowing you to complete them as you like and getting different endings. Main quests also offer you multiple ways to complete them, but never change where the story is going, only how. Surprisingly, failing a main quest is not a game over (at least not always), the story still progresses in a slightly different way, but you still get to the same point.

The gameplay is something special. Since you play the role of a blacksmith's son, you are completely illiterate. This means you need to learn how to live. You will have some teaching at the beginning, but for most of the adventure you will be on your own. Character growth and progression are tied to your actions, so you can only learn by doing. You don't know how to read, how to ride a horse, how to fight with a sword, how to shoot with a bow. Everything will need time, practice and hard work.

Similarly, you don't own anything in this world. You are not rich, you don't have a horse, a sword or an armor. Heck, you don't even have enough food, so you are probably going to die of starvation in a couple of days. You need to obtain everything on your own, either by completing quests and buying what you need or by stealing. Being a thief is quite difficult though. Robbing requires good timing and practice. Lockpicking is a nightmare, but they introduced an "easy lockpicking" mode which works better. If you are seen by witnesses they will run off to call guards, which will either make you pay a fine or put you in jail where you can wait or try to escape from (you can still convince them you did nothing wrong if you are skilled enough).

As you can see, the gameplay is real life slow on purpose cause it aims to be as realistic as possible. The more you learn, the more the game becomes easier and satisfying. Not many will like this choice of course, and if you consider Red Dead Redemption 2 "slow" then this will be even "slower" for you. I personally love this pacing. Yes, it takes more time compared to faster open world games, but the experience sticks more.

Speaking about open world, the map is huge and packed of content. Fortunately towns have their own fast travel points that unlock the first time you visit them, so it's easy to navigate once you find them all. Each town has a reputation system which depends entirely on your actions. Guards and citizens will remember you, especially if you were seen doing something illegal.

KC: Deliverance is also one of the best looking games running on CryEngine. Everything looks extremely sharp and detailed. Villages and towns look believable thanks to people having their own daily routines and castles are spectacular. Unfortunately there is still lot of texture pop-in, which can be annoying especially during dialogues. Loading times are awfully slow too, but it's partially understandable since basically every building interior can be explored (which is rarely allowed in games). At Ultra settings performance is decent enough, with a few bad frame drops in and there. UI is a bit unfriendly. Moving through each item in the inventory, checking stats and descriptions, character skills, quests log and such often made me feel uncomfortable. Many times I wanted to open the map but I opened the inventory instead.

Combat probably needed more polishing too. It's not [i] fun [/i] (I guess that's part of the realism), but enemies health bar is barely visible and the lock-on is terrible, only works properly when 1vs1, cause when you are surrounded by enemies it will often fail and you will be attacked from every side without being able to defend yourself. Also, there is no bow reticle (and no option to activate it), which maybe is too much even for a wanna-be realistic game.

Overall I would still recommend KC: Deliverance to those who are interested in RPGs with great well-written and performed stories and beautiful medieval settings, but again, it requires lot of time and patience. After 75 hours I completed the main story, most of the side quests (but not all) and partially some DLCs, so my journey is not over, there is still much to do and to discover.


[b] DLCs: [/b] They seem to be short, but very good, adding "more of the same" type of quests that can be completed in multiple ways. The only exception being "From the Ashes", which is basically a town building simulator and should be started as soon as possible 'cause it takes lot of time and money. And, for some weird reason, the game will force you to finish the "The Amorous Adventures of Bold Sir Hans Capon" DLC before being able to complete the main story. I suggest getting the Royal Edition for a better value, or Sir Hans Capon and Band of Bastards if you are only looking for a few more interesting quests.

[b] SPECIAL NOTE: [/b] KC: Deliverance is only the first part of the story. Developers planned a second game, which means that the ending of this one could leave a sour taste on some mouths. For me though it was an incredible experience, even if now I will be kinda forced to play the next one if I want to see how it really ends.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance is one of the best first-person RPGs to date. If you've ever wanted Skyrim but with more depth in the combat and RPG mechanics, this is the game for you.

First thing I tell everyone if they are considering grabbing it for themselves: the prologue is about 1-2 hours long, and it's not a very engaging introduction. However, once you get past the title card the game opens up and you can begin to enjoy the open world.

The game starts you with nothing, because you're a peasant. You're not the chosen one, you're not a skilled warrior. You're a peasant who can't even cut a stick with a sword. You can barely fight. You can't afford anything. You can't even read. Because of this, the game really makes you feel a sense of progression any time you improve your skills. Henry, your character, starts out as a weak, socially awkward, incompetent embarrassment of a man. As you progress however, he eventually becomes a bada*s protagonist you really root for.

Combat is difficult at first but remember, you're a peasant. Henry doesn't know how to fight, so his learning becomes your learning too. If you start out feeling that the combat is clunky, just remember that Henry just picked up a sword for the first time in his life. Would you know sword techniques if you were in his shoes? When Henry does begin to pick up on how to wield a weapon, the fighting is very satisfying. Unlike Skyrim, attacks have real weight to them. When you hit someone, you can tell they felt it.

I could say so much more but this recommendation is already long enough. If you like first-person RPGs, buy this game at any price, it's well worth it.

This is a fantastic game that I think gets misrepresented in a lot of reviews. It is NOT like the Witcher in any respect except you have a sword & Horse. Think of this as more of a medieval sim where you go about the life of a simple guy out to make it in the world after some pretty rough times. You are a peasant, and you are treated as such.
The Gameplay is fun, if you like the difficulty. It’s good to play a game where saving is rare & the consequences of your day-to-day can have some major impacts. You don’t enter into fights lightly as the combat has a sharp learning curve & is skill based, as well as being.. Well, deadly. Even later on as your skill increases, getting into combat will make you think it through before whipping out the sword. 
One thing I will also point out is the cut scenes. A few of these are rather long. This isn’t a complaint, on the contrary; just a warning.  I enjoyed them thoroughly. They are often fun & full of heart & round out your character beautifully. (One particular night of debauchery makes me laugh every time I think about it.)
On the whole, I can recommend this to anyone who enjoys sinking some time into a character & taking the time to appreciate the world they are in. Maybe even spending some time learning the rich lore of the area & era. And to people who don’t feel the need to be in combat all the time.
Sometimes it’s nice just to ride a horse through the forest & see what the world throws at you!

If you like slow-paced stories and non-fantasy worlds, this game is worth every moment. It's not a flawless game—you’ll find things to criticize if you're looking—but somehow, it ends up being incredibly lovable.
